{{Short description|Protagonist of a Japanese fairy tale}}
{{About|the Japanese folklore figure|the anime film based on it|Urashima Tarō (film)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2017}}
[[Image:Matsuki Heikichi(1899)-Urashima-p04.jpg|thumb|upright=2|Urashima Tarō and princess of Horai, by Matsuki Heikichi (1899)]]

{{nihongo|'''Urashima Tarō'''|浦島 太郎}} is the protagonist of a Japanese {{ill|Fairy tale|en|Fairy tale|WD=Q699|lt=Fairy tale|1=Fairy tale}} (''otogi banashi''), who, in a typical modern version, is a [[:en:fishermen|fisherman]] rewarded for rescuing a {{ill|Sea turtle|en|Sea turtle|WD=Q219329|lt=Sea turtle|1=Sea turtle}}, and carried on its back to the Dragon Palace ([[Ryūgū-jō]]) beneath the sea. There, he is entertained by the princess [[:en:Otohime|Otohime]]{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|name="miyao-on-otohime"}} as a reward. He spends what he believes to be several days with the princess. But when he returns to his home village, he discovers he has been gone for at least 100 years. When he opens the forbidden jewelled box ({{ill|Tamatebako|en|Tamatebako|WD=Q280383|lt=Tamatebako|1=Tamatebako}}), given to him by Otohime on his departure, he turns into an old man.

The tale originates from the legend of '''Urashimako''' ('''Urashima no ko''' or '''Ura no Shimako'''{{efn|Urashimako is the neutral designation; the name was often read as Urashima no ko in the past, but more recent commentators and editions in print prefer Ura no Shimako.}}) recorded in various pieces of literature dating to the 8th century, such as the ''[[Fudoki]]'' for {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}}, ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', and the ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}''.

During the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi|1=Muromachi period}} to {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}s, versions of ''{{ill|Urashima Tarō (otogi-zōshi)|en|Urashima Tarō (otogi-zōshi)|WD=Q49000995|lt=Urashima Tarō|1=Urashima Tarō (otogi-zōshi)}}'' appeared in storybook form called the ''[[:en:Otogizōshi|Otogizōshi]]'', made into finely painted picture scrolls and picture books or mass-printed copies. These texts vary considerably, and in some, the story ends with Urashima Tarō transforming into a crane.

Some iconic elements in the modern version are relatively recent. The portrayal of him riding a turtle dates only to the early 18th century, and while he is carried underwater to the Dragon Palace in modern tellings, he rides a boat to the princess's world called [[:en:Hōrai|Hōrai]] in older versions.

== Folktale or fairy tale ==

The Urashima Tarō tale familiar to most Japanese follows the storyline of children's tale author {{illm|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} in the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}. A condensed version of Sazanami's retelling then appeared in {{illm|Kokutei kyōkasho{{!}}''Kokutei kyōkasho''|ja|国定教科書}}, Japan's nationally designated textbook for elementary school, and became widely read by schoolchildren of the populace.{{Efn|Holmes, p. 6: "Miura solves the question of who the author of this Urashima Tarō [textbook] version was, and identifies him as Iwaya Sazanami".<ref name=holmes-p6&miura-p21>{{harvp|Holmes|2014|pp=6–7}} citing {{harvp|Miura|1989|p=21}}</ref>}} Modern versions of Urashima Tarō, which are generally similar, are demonstrably based on the story from this nationally designated textbook series.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Urashima tale first appeared in the 2nd edition ''Kokugo tokuhon'' or "National Language Reader", officially called ''Dai-2 ki Jinjō shōgaku tokuhon'' 第2期尋常小学読本 and unofficially known by the shorthand ''hatatako tokuhon'' ハタタコ読本. The story bore the title ''Urashima no hanashi'' (ウラシマノハナシ).{{sfnp|Miura|1989|pp=21, 34–35}} }}<ref name=holmes-p6&miura-p21/><ref>{{harvp|McKeon|1996|pp=195–196}}</ref>

== Plot ==
One day, a young fisherman named Urashima Tarō is fishing when he notices a group of children torturing a small turtle. Tarō saves it and lets it go back to the sea. The next day, a huge turtle approaches him and tells him that the small turtle he had saved is the daughter of the Emperor of the Sea, [[Ryūjin]], who wants to see him to thank him. The turtle magically gives Tarō gills and brings him to the bottom of the sea, to the Palace of the Dragon God ([[Ryūgū-jō]]). There he meets the Emperor and the small turtle, who was now a lovely princess, [[:en:Otohime|Otohime]].{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|name="miyao-on-otohime"|Oto-hime must have been the second daughter or the younger princess, since her name Oto can be read as ''otsu'', meaning "No. 2", as in the common phrase {{illm|kōotsu|ja|甲乙丙|lt=''kōotsu''}} which means "No. 1 and No. 2"," as explained by folklorist {{illm|Yoshio Miyao|ja|宮尾與男}}.{{sfnp|Miyao|2009|p=198}}}} The palace had a view to the four seasons, a different one on each side. Tarō stays there with Otohime for three days, but soon wants to go back to his village and see his aging mother, so he requests permission to leave. The princess says she is sorry to see him go, but wishes him well and gives him a mysterious box called ''{{ill|Tamatebako|en|Tamatebako|WD=Q280383|lt=Tamatebako|1=Tamatebako}}'' which will protect him from harm but which she tells him never to open. Tarō grabs the box, jumps on the back of the same turtle that had brought him there, and soon is at the seashore.

When he goes home, everything has changed. His home is gone, his mother has vanished, and the people he knew are nowhere to be seen. He asks if anybody knows a man called Urashima Tarō. They answer that they had heard someone of that name had vanished at sea long ago. He discovers that 300 years have passed since the day he left for the bottom of the sea. Struck by grief, he absent-mindedly opens the box the princess had given him, from which bursts forth a cloud of white smoke. He is suddenly aged, his beard long and white, and his back bent. From the sea comes the sad, sweet voice of the princess: "I told you not to open that box. In it was your old age ...".

== Commonly known version ==
[[File:Jinjyoshogakukokugotokuhon-v3-p040.jpg|thumb|360px|Urashima Taro encounters children on the beach who are "toying with" a turtle.{{right|―''Jinjō shōgaku kokugo tokuhon'' (the 3rd edition of ''Kokutei tokuhon'') (1928)}}]]

A summary of the Urashima tale from one of the nationalized textbooks ({{illm|Kokutei kyōkasho{{!}}''Kokutei kyōkasho''|ja|国定教科書}}) will be given below. The base text used will be ''Urashima Tarō'' (うらしま太郎), from the 3rd edition of the {{illm|Kokugo tokuhon{{!}}''Kokugo tokuhon''|ja|国語読本}} or "national language reader", a widely familiar textbook used during the 1918–1932 period.{{r|suzuki-t}}{{r|miura-21}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The 3rd edition was officially titled {{nihongo|''Jinjō shōgaku kokugo tokuhon''|尋常小学国語読本}} or "Elementary School National Language Reader". It was also known by its nickname {{illm|Hanahato tokuhon{{!}}''Hanahato tokuhon''|ja|ハナハト読本}} and other known as the "White Reader".{{r|suzuki-t}}}}<ref>{{harvp|Holmes|2014|pp=6–7, 77}}</ref> An English translation has been provided in Yoshiko Holmes's thesis.<ref>{{harvp|Holmes|2014|pp=151–152}}: as primary source No. 13.</ref>{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The title is mixed {{ill|Hiragana|en|Hiragana|WD=Q48332|lt=Hiragana|1=Hiragana}} and {{ill|Kanji|en|Kanji|WD=Q82772|lt=Kanji|1=Kanji}} in the 3rd edition. In the 2nd edition it was entirely in {{ill|Katakana|en|Katakana|WD=Q82946|lt=Katakana|1=Katakana}}. Although the story in the 2nd edition was earlier, Miura's analysis concentrated on the 3rd edition, as it was more widely read.}}

{{Quote|text=Long ago, a man named Urashima Tarō of unidentified profession{{efn|The 3rd edition national textbook begins "むかし、うらしま太郎といふ人 (Long ago, a person named Urashima Tarō)".}}<ref name=kokutei3 /> (or, in recent textbooks often a fisherman{{sfnp|Nakashima|2010|p=67}}) found a turtle on the beach being toyed with by a group of children. He purchased the turtle and released it in the ocean.

Two or three days later, while he was fishing on a boat as always, the grateful turtle came and told him he would carry him on his back to the underwater Dragon Palace ([[Ryūgū-jō|Ryūgū]]<ref>{{harvp|Holmes|2014|pp=151–152}} gives "Sea Palace" but the name "Ryūgū" is tabulated on p. 105 (under #13).</ref>). At the palace, the princess ([[:en:Otohime|Otohime]]<ref>{{harvp|Holmes|2014|pp=151–152}} gives "princess" but the name "Otohime" is tabulated on p. 104 (under #13).</ref>) thanked him for saving the turtle.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The 4th phase textbook adds that he was entertained by dances performed by ''{{ill|Pagrus major|en|Pagrus major|WD=Q1196387|lt=tai|1=Pagrus major}}'' (snapper), ''[[:en:hirame|hirame]]'' (halibut), {{ill|Octopus|en|Octopus|WD=Q40152|lt=octopuses|1=Octopus}} and other creatures.<ref name=kokutei4 /> The ''tai'' and ''hirame'' fish feature in the school song.}}

After an unspecified number of days, remembrance of his mother and father made him homesick, and he bid farewell to Otohime. The princess tried to dissuade him from leaving, but finally let him go with a parting gift, a mysterious box called ''{{ill|Tamatebako|en|Tamatebako|WD=Q280383|lt=Tamatebako|1=Tamatebako}}''<ref>{{harvp|Holmes|2014|pp=151–152}} gives "treasure box" but the name "tamatebako" is tabulated on p. 107 (under #13.).</ref> whose lid he was told never to open.

When Tarō returned to his hometown, everything had changed. His home was gone, his mother and father had perished, and the people he knew were nowhere to be seen. After not remembering the princess's warning, he lifted the lid of the box. A cloud of white smoke arose, turning him to a  white-haired old man.<ref name=kokutei3>{{citation|author=Japanese Ministry of Education  |title=Jinjō shōgaku kokugo tokuhon, kan 3 |script-title=ja:尋常小學國語讀本. 卷3 |publisher=Nihon Shoseki |year=1928  |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1874185 |pages=39–46}}</ref><ref>{{harvp|Miura|1989|pp=22ff.}}: reprint from  ''Dai 3 ki kokutei kyōkasho''</ref>|sign=|source=}}

The story remained as one of the dozen tales included in the 4th edition of national language reader textbooks also known as {{illm|Sakura tokuhon{{!}}''Sakura tokuhon''|ja|サクラ読本}} used from 1933 to c. 1940, thus continuing to enjoy wide recognition; for this reason ''Urashima'' could be considered one of the core stories of the so-called Japanese "national fairy tales".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Antoni |first=Klaus |title=Momotaro and the Spirit of Japan |journal=Asian Folklore Studies |volume=50 |year=1991 |pages=160–161 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/270376519}}</ref>

== School song ==
A number of renditions exist, where they are set to music. Among the most popular is the school song "Urashima Tarō" (浦島太郎) of 1911 which begins with the line "''Mukashi, mukashi Urashima wa, tasuketa kame ni tsurerarete'' (Long long ago was Urashima, by the turtle he rescued taken to the sea)", printed in the  {{illm|Jinjō shōgaku shōka{{!}}''Jinjō shōgaku shōka''|ja|尋常小学唱歌}} (1911).<ref>{{citation|last=Takasaki |first=Midori  |title=The Description of Otohime in Modern Literature |year=2010  |pages=164|publisher=Ochanomizu University |hdl=10083/49274 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www3.u-toyama.ac.jp/niho/song/urashimataro/urashimataro_e.html |last=Hamada |first=Miwa |title=Urashima-taro (Ministry of Education song)|website=Japanese Songs- Classified by Title – |year=2004 |access-date=2017-09-29}}</ref> This song's author was long relegated to anonymity, but the lyricist is now considered to be {{illm|Okkotsu Saburō|ja|乙骨三郎}}.<ref>{{citation|last=Ono |first=Mitsuyasu (小野恭靖) |title=Kodomo uta wo manabu hito no tame ni |script-title=ja:子ども歌を学ぶ人のために |publisher=Sekaishisosha |year=2007 |pages=229, 262|isbn=9784790712305 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JrE0AQAAIAAJ|language=ja}}</ref>{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=211}}

Another school song "Urashima Tarō" (うらしまたろう, lyrics by {{illm|Ishihara Wasaburō|ja|石原和三郎}} and music by {{illm|Tamura Torazō|ja|田村虎蔵}}) appeared in the ''Yōnen shōka'' (1900).{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=211}} Although written in stilted [[:en:Classical Japanese language|classical language]], Miura considered this version the more familiar.{{sfnp|Miura|1989|pp=36–37|ps=}}

== Otogizōshi ==
{{Main|Urashima Tarō (otogi-zōshi)}}
Long before the versions in 19th century textbooks, there had been the ''[[otogi-zōshi]]'' versions from the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}}.<ref name="holmes-p6&miura-p21" /> Conventionally, commentators using the term ''otogizōshi'' are referring by default to the text found in the ''Otogi Bunko'' (or "Companion Library"), since it was printed and widely disseminated.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The ''Otogi Bunko'' usually refers to the Shibukawa Collection, c. 1720, but the color-illustrated book called ''tanroku-bon'' dated 50 years earlier carries the same text.<ref name="keene" />}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|p=17}}{{sfnp|Holmes|2014|p=17, note 71}}

=== Otogi Bunko ===
In the ''Otogi Bunko'' (or "Companion Library") version, a young fisherman named Urashima Tarō catches a turtle on his fishing line and releases it. The next day, Urashima encounters a boat with a woman on it wishing to be escorted home. She does not identify herself, although she is the transformation of the turtle that was spared.{{efn|She only reveals this when Urashima wants to leave the Dragon Palace.}} When Urashima rows her boat to her magnificent residence, she proposes that they marry.<ref name=waterhouse /> The residence is the Dragon Palace, and on the four sides of the palace, each gardenscape is in a different season.<ref name=shirane /> Urashima decides to return to his home after three years and is given a {{Nihongo|memento box|かたみの筥/箱|katami no hako}} in parting.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|name=tamatebako-in-bunko|However the box is called ''tamatebako'' in the ''Otogi Bunko'' version, not in the main text, but in the inserted poem that contains the expression "'''akete kuyashiki'''" which later led to the stock phrase "{{Nihongo|opened to his regret(mortification), the tamatebako|開けて悔しき玉手箱|akete kuyashiki tamatebako}}" which has become well-known in association with the Urashima tale.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=111, 114}} This poem is quoted not just in the Otogi Bunko and all the Group IV texts,<ref>Hayashi (2012), ''Bulletin'' '''26''', p.10</ref> but in Group I also.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|p=10}}}} He arrives in his hometown to find it desolate, and discovers 700 years have passed since he last left it. He cannot restrain his temptation to open the box which he was cautioned not to open,<ref name=waterhouse /> whereupon three wisps of purple cloud appear and turn him into an old man.<ref name=waterhouse /> It ends with Urashima Tarō transforming into a crane,<ref>{{harvp|Sugiyama|1964}}</ref> and his wife reverting to the form of a turtle, the two thereafter revered as ''{{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|WD=Q5369590|lt=Myōjin|1=Myōjin}}'' ([[Shinto]] deities).<ref>{{citation|last=Watanabe |first=Masako |title=Storytelling in Japanese Art |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=2011 |url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=1588394409 |pages=66–67, 108}}</ref><ref name="otogi-bunko-textimage">{{citation|editor1-last=Imaizumi |editor1-first=Sadasuke (今泉定助) |editor2-last=Hatakeyama |editor2-first=Ken (畠山健)|title=Chapter 21: Urashimatarō |script-title=ja:浦島太郎|work=Otogizōshi 御伽草子 |volume=2 |publisher=Yoshikawa Hanshichi |year=1891 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/992892/92}} (text image)  {{in lang|ja}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cscd.osaka-u.ac.jp/user/rosaldo/Taro_Urashima.html |title=Taro Urashima story: A Fable |website=Ikeda Mitsuho |author=Ikeda Mitsuho |year=2013 |access-date=2017-09-24}} (transcribed) {{in lang|ja}}</ref>

=== Variants and groups ===
There are over 50 texts of the Urashima Tarō ''otogi-zōshi'' extant. These variants fall into four broad groups, clustered by their similarity.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|p=4}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2013|p=5}} The ''Otogi Bunko'' text belongs to Group IV.{{efn|Also both the picture scroll and the storybook in the {{ill|Columbia University|en|Columbia University|WD=Q49088|lt=Columbia University|1=Columbia University}} Library collection are Group IV.}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=20, 30}}

=== Group closest to modern version ===
[[File:Urashima Taro handscroll from Bodleian Library 1.jpg|thumbnail|right|480px|Urashima saves the turtle.{{right|{{small|―From an ''Otogizōshi'' picture scroll in the Bodleian Library collection,{{efn|name="bodleina-shelfmark"|MS. Jap. c. 4 (R)}} late 16th or early 17th century.}}}}]]

The ''Otogi Bunko'' version, despite its conventional status as the type text, differs considerably from the typical children's storybook published in the modern day: the protagonist neither purchases the turtle from others to save it, nor rides the turtle.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|p=17}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Urashima did not ride the turtle until the early 18th century.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2001|p=41}}}}

Group I texts are more similar to the modern version, as it contains the element of Urashima purchasing the turtle to save it.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|p=1}} Additionally, this group explicitly gives the princess's name as Otomime (or "Kame-no-Otohime"){{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=10, 14}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=10, 14}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=9, 25}} whereas she remains unnamed in the ''Otogi Bunko'' group. And the expression ''{{ill|Tamatebako|en|Tamatebako|WD=Q280383|lt=Tamatebako|1=Tamatebako}}'' or "jeweled hand-box" familiar to modern readers is also seen in the main text of Group I, and not the other groups (the interpolated poem excepted).{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|name=tamatebako-in-bunko}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2013|pp=11, 28, 30}}{{sfnp|Hayashi|2016|pp=10–11}}

The picture scroll in the collection of the {{ill|Bodleian Library|en|Bodleian Library|WD=Q82133|lt=Bodleian Library|1=Bodleian Library}}, Oxford University{{efn|name="bodleina-shelfmark"}} also belongs to Group I.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=4–5}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The full text is transcribed in Japanese, published in {{harvp|Hayashi|2013|pp=18–31}}.}}

Hayashi Kouhei has highlighted the characteristics of the Group I texts as follows: 1) Urashima purchases a turtle caught by others, 2) Boat arrives to convey him to [[:en:Horai|Horai]], 3) The four seasons assuage rather than provoke his homesickness,{{efn|That is, it is opposite the situation in Group I.}} 4) The villagers in recognition of his longevity give him proper {{ill|Cremation|en|Cremation|WD=Q207315|lt=Cremation|1=Cremation}},{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|And a Buddhist {{ill|Sādhanā|en|Sādhanā|WD=Q507662|lt=training priest|1=Sādhanā}} plays a role in convincing the villagers. This priest says Urashima lived 7000 years in the Takayasu, Keio, and Paris texts.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|p=13}} The {{ill|Japanese Folk Crafts Museum|en|Japanese Folk Crafts Museum|WD=Q3789149|lt=Nihon Mingeikan|1=Japanese Folk Crafts Museum}} copy is a hybrid since it gives "700 years" here instead, and "Dragon Palace ([[:en:Ryūgū|Ryūgū]])" rather than "Horai".{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=13, 14}}}} 5) Smoke from the ''tamatebako'' reaches Horai and Princess Otohime is grief-stricken.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2011|pp=9–10}}

== Other modern versions ==
=== Seki's version in English ===
The tale of "Urashima Taro" in {{ill|Keigo Seki|en|Keigo Seki|WD=Q6383606|lt=Keigo Seki|1=Keigo Seki}}'s anthology (translated into English 1963), was a version told in {{ill|Nakatado District, Kagawa|en|Nakatado District, Kagawa|WD=Q1206155|lt=Nakatado District, Kagawa|1=Nakatado District, Kagawa}}. In this variant, Urashima is localized as being from "Kitamae Oshima". It incorporates both the motif of the turtle being caught while fishing, and that of Urashima transforming into a crane at the end, which are found in the ''Otogizōshi''.

Here, it was a {{nihongo|three-tiered jeweled hand-box|三重ねの玉手箱|mitsugasane no tamatebako}}, that is to say, a stacked box that was given to Urashima. When he opened the lid, the first box (on the top) contained a {{ill|Crane (bird)|en|Crane (bird)|WD=Q25365|lt=crane|1=Crane (bird)}}'s feather, and the second a puff of white smoke that turned him into an old man, and the third a mirror, which made him see for himself that he had suddenly grown old. The feather from the first box then attached itself to his back, and Urashima flew up to the sky, encircling his mother's grave.<ref>{{harvp|Seki|1963|pp=111–114}}, reprinted in: {{harvp|Tatar|2017|pp=167–171}}</ref>

=== Versions retold in English ===
The story entitled "The Fisher-boy Urashima" (1886) retold by {{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}}, was number 8 in the "Japanese Fairy Tale Series",{{sfnp|Chamberlain|1886}}<ref name="chamberlain-tr-miyao-ed"/> printed by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō|1=Hasegawa Takejirō}}, the issuer of many such ''chirimen-bon'' or "crepe-paper books".<ref name=sharf /> Although the illustrations are not credited in the publication, they have been attributed to {{ill|Kobayashi Eitaku|en|Kobayashi Eitaku|WD=Q2784105|lt=Kobayashi Eitaku|1=Kobayashi Eitaku}}.<ref name=tablada /><ref name=kyoto-u-foreign-studies />

There is no single base text in Japanese identifiable, although it has been conjectured that Chamberlain adapted from "a popular version" and not straying far from it except adding explanatory or instructive passages for young readers.{{sfnp|Takanashi|1989|pp=121, 127}} Others have determined it must have been a composite consisting of older traditions from the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}'', combined with the near-modern Otogizōshi storybook plot,{{sfnp|Satomi|2001|p=100}} Chamberlain preferring to incorporate details from the ancient texts, while eschewing embellishment from the Otogizōshi.{{sfnp|Makino|2011|p=129}} Chamberlain has also published a {{ill|Verse (poetry)|en|Verse (poetry)|WD=Q1661|lt=versified|1=Verse (poetry)}} version of the tale.<ref name=chamberlain&mason/>

In Chamberlain's fairytale version, "Urashima" (not "Tarō") catches a tortoise (''{{ill|Sic|en|Sic|WD=Q192003|lt=Sic|1=Sic}}''){{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|It has been pointed out that while "tortoise" can be a turtle or a land turtle, the "{{ill|tortoiseshell|en|tortoiseshell|WD=Q2141546|lt=tortoiseshell|1=Tortoiseshell}}" of Japan is ''bekko'',{{sfnp|Takanashi|1989|p=124}} and this normally signifies a product taken from the shell of the [[hawksbill sea turtle]].}} while fishing on his boat, and releases it. The tortoise reappears in her true form as the Sea-God's daughter, and invites him to the Dragon Palace.{{Efn|Here, the Dragon Palace is not submerged in the ocean; the two of them reach it rowing by boat.}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The halls of the four season are lacking in the Dragon Palace here.{{sfnp|Makino|2011|p=100}}}}

There the couple are married and live happily for 3 years, but Urashima misses seeing his parents and his brothers. The Dragon Princess reluctantly allows him to leave, giving him a box he is instructed never to open, for it will cause him never to be able to return to the palace. When he returns to his home village, his absence turns out to have been 400 years. Urashima now wishes to go back to the Dragon Palace but he does not know the means, and opens the box. He turns into a white-haired, wrinkled old man and dies.<ref>{{harvp|Chamberlain|1886}}, ''The Fisher-boy Urashima''</ref> The ending by death concurs with older tradition,{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The ''Nihon Shoki'', the ''Fudoki'' of Tango Province, and the ''Man'yōshū''.{{sfnp|Makino|2011|p=129}}}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The death occurs in summer, in keeping with the ''Nihon Shoki'' which dates it to the seventh month of the 22nd year of Emperor Yuryaku.}} and not the ''otogi-zōshi'' storybook.{{sfnp|Makino|2011|p=129}}

{{ill|Lafcadio Hearn|en|Lafcadio Hearn|WD=Q313638|lt=Lafcadio Hearn|1=Lafcadio Hearn}}, who lived in Japan and translated or adapted many ghost stories from the country, rewrote the Urashima tale under the title "{{ill|The Dream of a Summer Day|en|The Dream of a Summer Day|WD=Q7730948|lt=The Dream of a Summer Day|1=The Dream of a Summer Day}}" in the late 19th century, working off of a copy of Chamberlain's "Japanese Fairy Tale Series" version.<ref>{{cite book|last=Hearn |first=Lafcadio |title=Out of the East: Reveries and Studies in New Japan |location=Boston and New York|publisher=Houghton, Mifflin |year=1895 |url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924021575208 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/cu31924021575208/page/n12 1]–27}}</ref>

=== Variations ===
As always with folklore, there are many different versions of this story.

There are other versions that add a further epilogue explaining the subsequent fate of Urashima Tarō after he turns into an old man. In one, he falls to dust and dies, in another, he transforms into a {{ill|Crane (bird)|en|Crane (bird)|WD=Q25365|lt=crane|1=Crane (bird)}} and flies up to the sky. In another, he grows gills and leaps into the sea, whereby he regains his youth.<ref name=sherman>{{citation|last=Sherman |first=Howard J  |title=World Folklore for Storytellers: Tales of Wonder, Wisdom, Fools, and Heroes |publisher=Routledge |year=2014 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Bi7fBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA216 |pages=215–216|isbn=9781317451648  }}</ref>

In another version Urashima ate a magic pill that gave him the ability to breathe underwater. In another version, he is swept away by a storm before he can rescue the turtle.

In another version, Irashima does stay with Otohime and they conceive a child. [https://yokai.com/otohime/]

== History ==
The full name Urashima Tarō was not given to the character until the 15th century (the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period|1=Muromachi period}}), first appearing in a genre of illustrated popular fiction known as ''[[:en:Otogizōshi|Otogizōshi]]'',{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=134–136ff}}<ref name=waterhouse /> and in the [[kyōgen]] play adaptation.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=102–107ff}}

The story itself can be found in much older sources, dating to the 8th century (the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}}), where the protagonist is styled either "Urashima no ko" or "Ura (no) Shimako", attested in earlier sources such as the ''[[Fudoki]]'' for {{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}} ({{small|''[[Tango no Kuni Fudoki]]'', [[:ja:丹後国風土記|丹後国風土記]]}}) that survived in excerpts, the ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=7–8, 28, 35}}

More recent editions of these texts tend to favor the "Ura (no) Shimako" reading,{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=7–9, 248}} although some consider this debatable.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The recent "Shimako" reading is based on the alternative name given as "Tsutsukawa no Shimako (Shimako of Tsutsukawa)" in the Tango Province [[Fudoki]] excerpt, which a number of scholars consider the oldest record. However, the same source also records the poem allegedly by the hero which clearly gives the reading in phonetics (in ''{{ill|Man'yōgana|en|Man'yōgana|WD=Q862803|lt=Man'yōgana|1=Man'yōgana}}'') as "Urashima-no-ko (宇良志麻能古)". The proponents of the other reading discount the poem by assuming it to be of a later date.<ref name="hayashi-kundoku"/>}}<ref name="hayashi-kundoku"/>

It has also been proposed that it was not until the Heian Period that the misreading "Urashima (no) ko" became current, because names with the suffix ''-ko'' ("child") came to be regarded as female, even though it once applied to either gender.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=107, 228}} When the texts were written for the [[kyōgen]] theatre, the character's name underwent further change to Urashima Tarō, with ''-tarō'' ("great youth") being a common suffix in male names.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=102–107ff}} Or perhaps the name was borrowed from {{illm|Tarō kaja|ja|太郎冠者}} who is a {{ill|Stock character|en|Stock character|WD=Q636497|lt=Stock character|1=Stock character}} in kyōgen.<ref name=sakamoto-annot-miyoshi/>

===Dragon Palace===
The ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}'' ballad mentions not only the woman of the Immortal Land, but her father as the Sea God ({{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|WD=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi|1=Watatsumi}}).<ref name=manyo-aston/><ref name=sakata/> Although this Sea God cannot be automatically equated with the Dragon God or Dragon King, due to the influence of the Chinese mythology of {{ill|Nine sons of the dragon|en|Nine sons of the dragon|WD=Q836090|lt=Nine Offspring of the Dragon|1=Nine sons of the dragon}} in the [[:en:Tang period|Tang period]], it has been speculated that the turtle princess must have been the Dragon King's daughter in even those early versions.<ref name=sakata/>

The otherworld Urashima visited was not the "Dragon Palace" ([[Ryūgū-jō|Ryūgū]]) until the ''[[otogi-zōshi]]'' versions appeared.<ref name=akiya/> The heroine then became Otohime, the younger daughter of the Dragon King.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=136}}

===Relative dates===
As for the relative dating of these texts, an argument has been advanced that places the ''Fudoki'' version as the oldest.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|By proponents such as {{illm|Akihisa Shigematsu |ja|重松明久}} (p. 107) and Yū Mizuno 1:63, cited by McKeon.}} The argument dates the ''Tango fudoki'' to shortly after 715, but the compilers refer to an earlier record by {{illm|Iyobe no Umakai|ja|伊預部馬養}}, which was identical in content.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=7–8}}<ref name=shigematsu-oldest /><ref name=mizuno-oldest /> It has even been suggested by {{ill|Shūichi Katō (critic)|en|Shūichi Katō (critic)|WD=Q661802|lt=Shūichi Katō|1=Shūichi Katō (critic)}} that this Umakai originally adapted this tale into Japanese from a similar Chinese tale.<ref name=kato />

== Tango Fudoki ==
[[File:Gishi47zu-vol2-009-Gekko-zuihitsu-Mizunoe-no-Urashima.jpg|thumb|300px|Mizuenoe no Urashima riding a turtle with flowing tail (''mino game''{{sfnp|Hayashi|2001|p=43–45}}). Depiction of him riding a turtle appeared quite late, in the early 18th century.{{sfnp|Hayashi|2001|p=41}}<br />{{right|—{{ill|Ogata Gekkō|en|Ogata Gekkō|WD=Q2574296|lt=Ogata Gekkō|1=Ogata Gekkō}}, ''Gekkō zuihitsu'' (1887).{{sfnp|Hayashi|2001|p=33}}}}]]
In this version,{{Refn|Translated in full by Holmes;{{sfnp|Holmes|2014|pp=114–118}} also see Akima.{{sfnp|Akima|1993|pp=109–112}}}} the protagonist is referred to as "Urashimako{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Urashimako is the neutral form of convenience, it has been debated whether it should be read "Urashima no ko" or "Ura no Shimako".{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=7–9, 248}}<ref name="hayashi-kundoku"/>}} of Mizunoe" (or "Urashimako of {{illm|Tsutsukawa, Yosa District{{!}}Tsutsukawa|ja|筒川村}} in {{ill|Yosa District, Kyoto|en|Yosa District, Kyoto|WD=Q1078639|lt=Yosa-gun|1=Yosa District, Kyoto}}".

Urashimako catches a five-coloured turtle and keeps it in his boat, and during his sleep, the creature transforms into a beautiful woman.{{sfnp|Tagaya|2011|pp=98–99, 103, 107}} She identifies herself as someone from the household of immortals, and proposes to take him to the place of immortals,{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=44–47}} which may be Horaisan ({{ill|Mount Penglai|en|Mount Penglai|WD=Q798391|lt=Mount Penglai|1=Mount Penglai}}) or "Tokoyo-no-kuni" ("Timeless Land" or "Land of Eternity").{{efn|It is written as Horai ({{ill|Mount Penglai|en|Mount Penglai|WD=Q798391|lt=Mount Penglai|1=Mount Penglai}}) in the straight Chinese text, but it is also annotated to indicate its should be read as Tokoyo-no-kuni.}}{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=34, 65}}

They are greeted by first seven, then eight children, who represent the constellations of {{ill|Pleiades|en|Pleiades|WD=Q13423|lt=Pleiades|1=Pleiades}} and {{ill|Taurus (constellation)|en|Taurus (constellation)|WD=Q10570|lt=Taurus|1=Taurus (constellation)}} (or more precisely the {{ill|Hyades (star cluster)|en|Hyades (star cluster)|WD=Q13511|lt=Hyades|1=Hyades (star cluster)}} cluster)<ref name=ikeda-hiroko />{{sfnp|Holmes|2014|p=116}} who address him as the "husband of Kame Hime (Princess Turtle)".{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=10}}{{sfnp|Holmes|2014|p=116}} The remainder is mostly the same as the typical tale.<ref name=ikeda-hiroko />

After three years, the man develops a longing for his parents and homeland. The princess is saddened, but imparts him with a {{nihongo|jeweled comb box|玉匣|tamakushige}}, forbidding him to open it if he wished ever to return to her.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=12}} He returns and finds no trace of his home or family, except that he is remembered as a man who disappeared long ago, and would be over three hundred years old if still alive. Forgetting the promise, he opens the box, whereupon a beautiful figure like a fragrant orchid is carried away to the heavens with the clouds, and he realizes he can never meet the princess again.{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=13}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|An alternate reading is that a cloud rose up, and so too a certain sweet fragrance.{{sfnp|Tagaya|2011|pp=98–99, 103, 107}}}} Still, the couple are somehow (supernaturally) able to exchange poems.{{sfnp|Holmes|2014|pp=114–118}} These poems are recorded in phonetic ''{{ill|Man'yōgana|en|Man'yōgana|WD=Q862803|lt=Man'yōgana|1=Man'yōgana}}''.<ref name=hayashi-kundoku /><ref name=sasaki-ed />

==''Nihon Shoki''==
In the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', Urashimako of Mizunoe is mentioned in the entry for Autumn, 7th month the 22nd year of reign of {{ill|Emperor Yūryaku|en|Emperor Yūryaku|WD=Q357235|lt=Emperor Yūryaku|1=Emperor Yūryaku}}. [[William George Aston|Aston]]'s translation assigns this the year 478 A.D. The entry states that Urashimako (child Urashima, child of Urashima, etc.) of Mizunoe while fishing on a boat, caught a turtle which transformed into a woman. They went into the sea, and reached {{ill|Mount Penglai|en|Mount Penglai|WD=Q798391|lt=Mount Hōrai|1=Mount Penglai}} (glossed in ''{{ill|Kana|en|Kana|WD=Q187659|lt=Kana|1=Kana}}'' as Tokoyo<ref name=poulton/>), where they saw {{nihongo|immortals|仙衆 (ひじり)}}.{{sfnp|Aston|1896|loc='''1''', p. 368}}<ref name=bialock/>

As to the phrase that they go "into the sea" implies, the Mount Hōrai as conceived here may be a submarine island, a suggestion made by Japanese literature professor {{illm|Ōkuma Kiichirō|ja|大久間喜一郎}}.<ref name="okuma"/>

==Manyoshu==

A poem reflecting upon the legend of Urashima of Mizunoe occurs in the ''{{ill|Man'yōshū|en|Man'yōshū|WD=Q834321|lt=Man'yōshū|1=Man'yōshū}}''. The piece is ascribed to {{ill|Takahashi no Mushimaro|en|Takahashi no Mushimaro|WD=Q840963|lt=Takahashi no Mushimaro|1=Takahashi no Mushimaro}}.{{sfnp|Holmes|2014|p=23}} Early translations include the prose rendition by Aston,<ref name=manyo-aston/> and the ballad-form by Chamberlain.<ref name=manyo-chamberlain/>

In this version, the woman of the Immortal Land (Tokoyo) appears as the daughter of the Sea God ({{ill|Watatsumi|en|Watatsumi|WD=Q1474187|lt=Watatsumi no kami|1=Watatsumi}}).<ref name=manyo-aston/>{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|p=33}}

==Localizations==

=== Yokohama ===
[[Image:Keiunji -03.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.7|Keiun-ji, the stele that reads "Ryūgū denrai Urashima Kanzeon Urashima-tera", which used to be at Kampuku-ji.<ref name=kenkyukai1928/>]]

{{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Basil Hall Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}} (1880) indicated the presence of a temple dedicated to Urashima at {{ill|Kanagawa-ku, Yokohama|en|Kanagawa-ku, Yokohama|WD=Q1143712|lt=Kanagawa-ku, Yokohama|1=Kanagawa-ku, Yokohama}}, which housed several relics such as Urashima's fishing-line, and the casket (tamatebako).<ref name=manyo-chamberlain/> But when [[:en:Ernest Satow|Ernest Satow]] went there with Chamberlain on 2 May 1880, there was nothing left to see except the statue of [[Kannon|Kannon]] (Kanzeon), the {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva|1=Bodhisattva}} of mercy.<ref name=satow/>
[[File:Urashima-Kannon_Pavilion.jpg|thumb|Statues of Kannon, Urashima Tarō and Otohime enshrined at Keiun-ji, Yokohama.]]
Neither recorded the name to the temple, but Japanese sources write that the so-called Urashima-dera (Urashima Temple) used to be {{nihongo||観福寺|Kanpuku-ji}}, until it burned down in 1868,{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|One source says this was still during Keiō 4 in (1868)<ref name=inoue_osamu/> another wrote "27th day of 1st month of Meiji 1"<ref name=kenkyukai1928/> Japan decided that dates in Keio 4, be retroactively rewritten as dates in Meiji 1.}} and the temple, including the Kannon goddess statue got translated to {{nihongo||慶運寺|Keiun-ji}} in 1872.<ref name=inoue_osamu/><ref name=hayashi-kampukuji/>

The old Urashima-dera sat on a mountain top. There is a circulating pamphlet which shows the view of the harbor from this vantage point, depicting the fleet of {{ill|Black Ships|en|Black Ships|WD=Q1136943|lt=Black Ships|1=Black Ships}} led by {{ill|Matthew C. Perry|en|Matthew C. Perry|WD=Q61855|lt=Commodore Perry|1=Matthew C. Perry}}'s fleet in 1852–1854.<ref>{{citation|title=Tōkaidō Kanagawa urashima-dera sanjō ni okeru ikokusen hasso chōbō no kei |script-title=ja:東海道神奈川於浦島寺山上異國舩眺望之景 |trans-title=Eight American ships in Yokohama seen from the Urashima Temple |url=https://www.loc.gov/resource/cph.3g10365/}}</ref>

Local legend also claims native ties to Urashima Tarō, claiming that his father Urashima Tayū was originally from somewhere not far from Yokohama, in {{ill|Miura District, Kanagawa|en|Miura District, Kanagawa|WD=Q1203937|lt=Miura District, Kanagawa|1=Miura District, Kanagawa}} in Sagami Province. But the father moved to 
{{ill|Tango Province|en|Tango Province|WD=Q1054331|lt=Tango Province|1=Tango Province}}. This legend adds that when Urashima Tarō returned from the Dragon Place, he was guided to seek his parents' grave in "Shirahata, Musashi Province" (in today's Yokohama).

He finally found the grave, thanks to Princess Oto-hime who lit up an illuminating light on a pine branch.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|A pine named {{nihongo||龍燈の松|Ryūto no matsu|extra='dragon lantern pine'}}, which was this illuminated pine according to legend, stood until it was cut down when the railway opened.<ref name=kenkyukai1928/>}} Tarō built a hut to live here, housing the goddess statue from the Dragon Palace. The hut later became Kampuku-ji temple.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hagisaka |first=Noboru (萩坂昇) |title=Yokohama no minwa |script-title=ja:よこはまの民話|publisher=Musashi no jidō bunka no kai|year=1976 |series=Kanagawa no minwa|pages=97–103}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kojima |first=Yoshiyuki (小島瓔礼)|author-link=|title=Busō mukashi banashi shu: Kanagawa |script-title=ja:武相昔話集: 神奈川|publisher=Iwasaki Bijutsusha |year=1981|page=71}}</ref>

=== Okinawa ===
{{ill|Basil Hall Chamberlain|en|Basil Hall Chamberlain|WD=Q810029|lt=Chamberlain|1=Basil Hall Chamberlain}} noted the theory that the Dragon Palace might be a romanticized notion of Okinawa, since "[[Ryūgū-jo|Ryūgū]]" (Dragon Palace) and [[:en:Ryūkyū Islands|Ryūkyū]] (Okinawa) are near {{ill|Homophone|en|Homophone|WD=Q221079|lt=Homophone|1=Homophone}}s.<ref name=manyo-chamberlain/>

Recorded in {{nihongo||[[:ja:遺老説伝|遺老説伝]]|Irō setsuden|extra="Accounts Left by Old Men"}} of the 18th century, Tale 103 "A person of Yonaha village visits the Dragon Palace" is considered analogous to Urashima Tarō.<ref name=yanagita-okinawa/><ref name="urano&fukatsu"/><ref name=kurata/> In it, a certain man of Yonaha village in {{ill|Haebaru, Okinawa|en|Haebaru, Okinawa|WD=Q1206308|lt=Haebaru|1=Haebaru, Okinawa}} finds a lock of black hair and returns it to a beautiful maiden. She leads him to the Dragon Palace. Three months pass and the man wishes to return, but the goddess reveals 33 generations have already passed in his absence. The man receives a folded-up piece of paper he is forbidden from unwrapping, but he opens this packet and a piece of white hair clings to him, turning him into an old man, and he dies. He was enshrined at the place which was named Usani-daki, because the man had "sat and reposed" ({{lang|ja-Latn|usani}}) in his despair.<ref name="urano&fukatsu"/><ref name="taira"/>

Similar tales are found on [[:en:Miyako-jima|Miyako-jima]] and other places.{{sfnp|Yanagita|1971|p=50}} [[Kunio Yanagita|Yanagita Kunio]] felt that the notion of the Dragon Palace shared its origin with the concept of Niruya ({{illm|Niraikanai|ja|ニライカナイ}}) in the southerly islands of Japan.<ref name=yanagita-okinawa2/>

{{lang|ja-Latn|Irō setsuden}} also records a similar tale, number 42, about {{nihongo||善縄大屋子|Yoshinawa Fuyako}}, which describes a man who, bidden by a mysterious woman appeared before him, carried a large turtle to his home, which bit and gave him a terrible wound so that he was buried. But he turned out not to have died a mortals death, and lived on.<ref name=taira/><ref name=yanagita-okinawa2/>

=== Kiso, Nagano ===
{{Further|Nezame no toko}}
[[File:Kuniyoshi Station 38.jpg|right|thumb|upright=0.8|[[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]], {{lang|ja-Latn|{{ill|Fukushima-juku|en|Fukushima-juku|WD=Q3090713|lt=Fukushima-juku|1=Fukushima-juku}}}} (one of the {{ill|69 Stations of the Nakasendō|en|69 Stations of the Nakasendō|WD=Q741218|lt=69 stations|1=69 Stations of the Nakasendō}} of the [[:en:Kiso-kaidō|Kiso-kaidō]]).]]

Local legend has it that Urashima Tarō once dwelled in the mountains of Kiso, {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|WD=Q127877|lt=Nagano|1=Nagano Prefecture}}. This legend originated in near-modern times, from the late {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi|1=Muromachi period}} to {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}s.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wilson |first=William Scott |title=Walking the Kiso Road: A Modern-Day Exploration of Old Japan |publisher=Shambhala Publications |year=2015  |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=454DCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA135 |pages=135–141|isbn=9780834803176 }}</ref><ref name=torii/>

Although a contrived piece of fiction, the old-style ''{{ill|Jōruri (music)|en|Jōruri (music)|WD=Q1361891|lt=jōruri|1=Jōruri (music)}}'' {{nihongo||『浦嶋太郎』|Urashima Tarō}} situates its story in the vicinity of this local legend, namely [[:en:Agematsu, Nagano|Agematsu-juku]].{{efn|Agematsu-juku is actually adjacent to Fukushima-juku of Kuniyoshi's [[ukiyo-e]] painting.}} Urashima Tarō appears here as a child born after a local couple prays to [[Togakushi Shrine|Togakushi]] {{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|WD=Q5369590|lt=Myōjin|1=Myōjin}}. He and Tamayori-hime fall in love. She is very much a mortal, but after she commits suicide in Ina River (tributary of {{ill|Kiso River|en|Kiso River|WD=Q779607|lt=Kiso River|1=Kiso River}}), she becomes transformed into a supernatural being serving the Dragon Palace. A scale cloak lets her transform into a turtle, in which guise, she is reunited with Urashima Tarō who is fishing in Ina River. Note the "catching of the turtle" scene is transposed from ocean to a river in the mountains.<ref name=torii>{{citation|last=Torii |first=Fumiko (島居フミ子) |title=Kiso ni yomigaetta Urashima Tarō |script-title=ja:木曾に蘇った浦島太郎 |trans-title=Urashima Tarō revived in Kiso |journal=Nihon Bungaku |year=1992 |url=http://opac.library.twcu.ac.jp/opac/repository/1/4944/KJ00005527571.pdf |pages=32–43|language=ja}}</ref>

== Comparative mythology ==
The story bears varying degrees of similarity to folktales from other cultures. ''{{ill|Rip Van Winkle|en|Rip Van Winkle|WD=Q1129589|lt=Rip Van Winkle|1=Rip Van Winkle}}'' is the foremost familiar example, although strictly speaking this cannot be called a "folktale", since it is a fictional work by {{ill|Washington Irving|en|Washington Irving|WD=Q181667|lt=Washington Irving|1=Washington Irving}} loosely based on folklore.<ref name=seal&white /> Nevertheless, Urashima has been labeled the "Japanese Rip van Winkle", even in academic folkloristic literature.<ref name=mills /> "Urashima"{{efn|name=urashima-taro-jotai}} is also a Japanese metaphor similar to "Rip Van Winkle" for someone who feels lost in a world that has changed in their absence.<ref>Shin Wa-Ei Daijiten, 5th edition, entry "Urashima Tarō. Kenkyūsha. 2006.</ref>

This pair of tales may not be the closest matching among the motif group. Writing in the 19th century, {{ill|Lafcadio Hearn|en|Lafcadio Hearn|WD=Q313638|lt=Lafcadio Hearn|1=Lafcadio Hearn}} suggested that Irving wrote another piece called "The Adelantado of the Seven Cities", based on Portuguese tradition, which bore an even stronger resemblance to Urashima.<ref name=hearn-notes /> Japanese art collector {{ill|William Anderson (collector)|en|William Anderson (collector)|WD=Q1537815|lt=William Anderson|1=William Anderson (collector)}} also wrote that a certain Chinese tale was closer to "Rip Van Winkle" than Urashima was.<ref name=anderson />

That Chinese analogue is the anecdote of the woodcutter Wang Zhi,{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Wang Chih (王質<ref name=mayers />).}} who after watching [[:en:Chinese immortal|immortals]] playing a board game discovers many years have passed.<ref name=anderson /> The piece is a selection in the {{illm|Shuyiji (Ren Fang){{!}}''Shuyiji''|zh|述異記 (任昉)|ja|述異記}}{{efn|''Shu i Chi''}} or "Accounts of Strange Things", and is also known as the legend of {{ill|Ranka (legend)|en|Ranka (legend)|WD=Q6756934|lt=Lankeshan|1=Lanke (legend)}}{{efn|"Lan-k'o shan"}} or "Rotten Axe Handle Mountain".{{sfnp|Sugiyama|1964}}<ref name=wu-jtw-notes /> Sometimes this Chinese tale is conjectured as a possible actual source for Urashima, but there is lack of consensus among folklorists regarding their interrelationship.{{sfnp|Sugiyama|1964}}

Other cognate tales include the Irish legend of {{ill|Oisín|en|Oisín|WD=Q2016937|lt=Oisín|1=Oisín}}{{efn|Ossian}} who met {{ill|Niamh (mythology)|en|Niamh (mythology)|WD=Q2033813|lt=Niamh|1=Niamh (mythology)}} and spent his life with her in {{ill|Tír na nÓg|en|Tír na nÓg|WD=Q2463952|lt=Tír na nÓg|1=Tír na nÓg}},{{sfnp|McKeon|1996|pp=14–15}}<ref>{{harvp|Tagaya|2011|p=99}}, citing Doi, Shinwa 1973 pp. 19–25</ref><ref name=briggs /> and the Vietnamese {{ill|The Tale of Từ Thức Marrying a Goddess|en|The Tale of Từ Thức Marrying a Goddess|WD=Q10831877|lt=legend of Từ Thức|1=The Tale of Từ Thức Marrying a Goddess}}, who aids a goddess arrested for plucking a peony flower during a festival.<ref name=costineanu /> In both these cases, the hero is united with a goddess who dwells in a land beyond the sea. Từ Thức's story is collected in ''{{ill|Truyền kỳ mạn lục|en|Truyền kỳ mạn lục|WD=Q7848384|lt=Truyền kỳ mạn lục|1=Truyền kỳ mạn lục}}'' by {{ill|Nguyễn Dữ|en|Nguyễn Dữ|WD=Q10799084|lt=Nguyễn Dữ|1=Nguyễn Dữ}}.

The tale of Urashima Taro holds many similarities with tales of the international catalogue {{ill|Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index|en|Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index|WD=Q301545|lt=Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index|1=Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index}}, grouped under type ATU 681, "The Relativity of Time". A similar story is ''The Marsh King's Daughter'', a {{ill|literary fairy tale|en|literary fairy tale|WD=Q24723|lt=literary fairy tale|1=Literary fairy tale}} by {{ill|Hans Christian Andersen|en|Hans Christian Andersen|WD=Q5673|lt=Hans Christian Andersen|1=Hans Christian Andersen}}. However, Hiroko Ikeda's Japanese index of folktales lists ''Urashima Taro'' as type 470*, "The Dragon Palace" or "Urashima Taroo".<ref>Hiroko Ikeda. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=EPgZAAAAIAAJ&q=urashima A Type and Motif Index of Japanese Folk-Literature]''. Folklore Fellows Communications Vol. 209. Helsinki: Suomalainen Tiedeakatemia. 1971. pp. 119-120.</ref>

== Commemoration ==

A shrine on the western coast of the Tango Peninsula in northern {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, named Urashima Jinja, contains an old document describing a man, Urashimako, who left his land in 478 A.D. and visited a land where people never die. He returned in 825 A.D. with a {{ill|Tamatebako|en|Tamatebako|WD=Q280383|lt=Tamatebako|1=Tamatebako}}. Ten days later he opened the box, and a cloud of white smoke was released, turning Urashimako into an old man.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dragons, Demons and Deities: Folklore of the Kyoto by the Sea Area - Urashima Shrine, Ine|website=Another Kyoto - Official Travel Guide|date=8 December 2021|url=https://www.kyototourism.org/en/column/17773/#Urashima_Shrine_Ine|access-date=28 May 2023|archive-date=21 May 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230521152646/https://www.kyototourism.org/en/column/17773/|url-status=live}}</ref> Later that year, after hearing the story, {{ill|Emperor Junna|en|Emperor Junna|WD=Q374136|lt=Emperor Junna|1=Emperor Junna}} ordered {{ill|Ono no Takamura|en|Ono no Takamura|WD=Q1139928|lt=Ono no Takamura|1=Ono no Takamura}} to build a shrine to commemorate Urashimako's strange voyage, and to house the Tamatebako and the spirit of Urashimako.

== Adaptations ==
The animated adaptation ''[[:en:Urashima Tarō (anime)|Urashima Tarō]]'' of the tale, premiered in 1918, is among some of the oldest {{ill|Anime|en|Anime|WD=Q1107|lt=Anime|1=Anime}} created in Japan,<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/stories/2008/03/28/2201373.htm|title=90yo Japanese anime recovered|website=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=27 March 2008 }}</ref> the same year that Oz author {{ill|Ruth Plumly Thompson|en|Ruth Plumly Thompson|WD=Q449234|lt=Ruth Plumly Thompson|1=Ruth Plumly Thompson}} adapted it as "Urashima and the Princess of the Sea" for {{ill|Public Ledger (Philadelphia)|en|Public Ledger (Philadelphia)|WD=Q3410423|lt=The Philadelphia Public Ledger|1=Public Ledger (Philadelphia)}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hungrytigerpress.com/tigertales/tigertale060.shtml|title=Tiger Tales No. 60 – Urashima and the Princess of the Sea|website=www.hungrytigerpress.com|access-date=2017-07-31}}</ref>

The story influenced various works of fiction and a number of films. In 1945, Japanese writer {{ill|Osamu Dazai|en|Osamu Dazai|WD=Q317685|lt=Osamu Dazai|1=Osamu Dazai}} published ''Otogizōshi'' ("fairytale book"), which includes a much expanded version of the story. Urashima's tale, as the other three included in the ''Otogizōshi'', is used mostly as a platform for Dazai's own thoughts and musings. {{ill|Ursula K. Le Guin|en|Ursula K. Le Guin|WD=Q181659|lt=Ursula K. Le Guin|1=Ursula K. Le Guin}}'s short story "{{ill|A Fisherman of the Inland Sea|en|A Fisherman of the Inland Sea|WD=Q4401396|lt=A Fisherman of the Inland Sea|1=A Fisherman of the Inland Sea}}" (or "Another Story", 1994) is a reception of the Urashima story set in the [[:en:Ekumen|Ekumen]] or Hainish universe.

The story was adapted in Brazil in the 1960s for use in an advertising campaign by airline {{ill|Varig|en|Varig|WD=Q861197|lt=Varig|1=Varig}} to promote the first direct flights between {{ill|Rio de Janeiro|en|Rio de Janeiro|WD=Q8678|lt=Rio de Janeiro|1=Rio de Janeiro}} and {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. The campaign was produced by [[Lynxfilm]] and created by [[Ruy Perotti]]. The theme, sung by [[Rosa Miyake]], became famous throughout the country.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.estadao.com.br/noticias/geral,jingle-inspirado-em-lenda-de-urashima-taro-marcou-epoca,102615|title=Jingle inspirado em lenda de Urashima Taro marcou época|website=[[Estadão]]|access-date=2021-03-30}}</ref>

The {{ill|Ultra Q|en|Ultra Q|WD=Q2699578|lt=Ultra Q|1=Ultra Q}} episode title "Grow Up! Little Turtle" is largely based on Urashima Tarō's tale, along with elements of "{{ill|The Boy Who Cried Wolf|en|The Boy Who Cried Wolf|WD=Q1190945|lt=The Boy Who Cried Wolf|1=The Boy Who Cried Wolf}}" and the original ''{{ill|Gamera, the Giant Monster|en|Gamera, the Giant Monster|WD=Q1916669|lt=Gamera|1=Gamera, the Giant Monster}}'' film. In it, Tarō is a schoolboy given to making up stories who is trying to grow a turtle to 99cm, at which point he believes it will take him to the Dragon Palace.
